lead: Harmonic elimination chooses the switching angles of an inverter so that chosen low-order harmonics are exactly zero. Each harmonic is a Fourier coefficient, a sum of cosines of the switching angles, and setting it to zero gives one equation per harmonic. With N angles per quarter cycle one equation fixes the fundamental and the other N − 1 remove N − 1 harmonics. This is selective harmonic elimination (SHE). Only a few universities teach it as a separate topic. Pulse-width choice, notching, phase-shifted transformers and stepped waves are the classical ways to do it.
prereq: You need: the Fourier coefficients of a pulse from single and multiple pulse modulation.

sections.h3: A harmonic is an equation in the switching angles

blocks.text: Make the output quarter-wave symmetric: the second quarter mirrors the first and the negative half mirrors the positive half. Then all even harmonics and all cosine terms vanish, and only the odd sine coefficients b<sub>n</sub> remain. They depend only on the switching angles α<sub>1</sub> < α<sub>2</sub> < … < α<sub>N</sub> in the first quarter (0° to 90°).
bn = (4Vdc/nπ) Σ (−1)k+1 cos nαk This is for a three-level (unipolar) output that is zero from 0 to α1, +Vdc from α1 to α2, zero again from α2 to α3, and so on; n is odd.
bn = (4Vdc/nπ)[1 + 2Σ (−1)^k cos nαk] This is for a two-level (bipolar) output that starts at +Vdc and changes sign at each αk.

N angles give N equations: b<sub>1</sub> equal to the wanted fundamental and b<sub>n</sub> = 0 for N − 1 chosen harmonics. The equations are nonlinear, so they are solved offline (by Newton's method, for example) for each output level, and the angles are stored in a table that the controller reads.

items: Pulse width. A single pulse 2d wide has b<sub>n</sub> ∝ sin nd, which is zero when nd is a multiple of 180°: a 120° pulse removes the 3rd, and a 72° or 144° pulse the 5th. This is the one-angle case, α<sub>1</sub> = 90° − d.
Notching. Extra notches in each quarter of a square wave give extra angles: two notches can remove the 3rd and 5th while the fundamental stays near the square-wave value.

Phase-shifted transformers. Two square-wave bridges displaced by φ and added in series transformer windings give b<sub>n</sub> ∝ cos(nφ/2): φ = 60° removes the 3rd and φ = 36° the 5th. In three-phase, two six-step bridges feeding star and delta windings (30° apart) cancel the 5th and 7th, leaving the 11th and 13th: a twelve-step wave.
Stepped waves. Several bridges or cells with their own sources add up to a staircase; choosing each step angle removes harmonics, as in multilevel inverters.

blocks.text: Removing low harmonics does not destroy their energy. It moves to the next orders, which a small filter or the load inductance handles more cheaply because their impedance is n times larger.

In a three-phase three-wire system the triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, 15th) are the same in all three phases and cancel in the line voltage, so no angle is spent on them. A three-phase SHE table removes the 5th, 7th, 11th and 13th instead. Compared with an output filter, SHE removes the harmonic at the source with a low switching frequency, which suits high-power drives. Its costs: the angles are fixed for each operating point, a change of output needs a jump to another row of the table, and closely spaced angles need a minimum pulse width the devices can make.

examples.question: A full bridge with V<sub>dc</sub> = 220 V gives a three-level output with one switching angle per quarter, α<sub>1</sub> = 30° (output zero from 0° to 30°, then +V<sub>dc</sub> to 90°). Find b<sub>1</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>, b<sub>5</sub> and b<sub>7</sub>. Which harmonic has been eliminated?
steps: The output is a 120° pulse in each half cycle, so the 3rd harmonic (and the 9th, cos 270° = 0) is eliminated; the 5th and 7th remain at 20 % and 14 % of the fundamental.
examples.answer: b<sub>1</sub> = 242.6 V, b<sub>3</sub> = 0, b<sub>5</sub> = −48.5 V and b<sub>7</sub> = −34.7 V peak; the 3rd harmonic is eliminated.

examples.question: The same 220 V bridge runs a two-level square wave with two notches per quarter, at α<sub>1</sub> = 23.64° and α<sub>2</sub> = 33.33°. Show that the 3rd and 5th harmonics are eliminated and find b<sub>1</sub>, b<sub>7</sub> and b<sub>9</sub>.
steps: For two angles, b<sub>n</sub> = (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ)(1 − 2 cos nα<sub>1</sub> + 2 cos nα<sub>2</sub>).
examples.answer: The 3rd and 5th are zero; b<sub>1</sub> = 235.0 V, b<sub>7</sub> = 69.7 V and b<sub>9</sub> = 114.6 V peak. The removed energy reappears at the 7th and 9th.

traps: N angles remove N − 1 harmonics, not N: one equation is used up by the fundamental.
Never spend an angle on an even harmonic: quarter-wave symmetry already removes them.
Use the formula that matches the waveform. Three-level and two-level outputs have different b<sub>n</sub> expressions.
Triplens cancel in the line voltage of a three-wire system, not in the phase-to-midpoint voltage.

quiz.q: What does selective harmonic elimination set to zero?
quiz.a: Chosen low-order harmonic coefficients b<sub>n</sub>, by choosing the switching angles.

quiz.q: Why do N angles per quarter remove only N − 1 harmonics?
quiz.a: N angles give N equations; one fixes the fundamental and N − 1 are left for harmonics.

quiz.q: Find the widest single pulse that removes the 5th harmonic, and its fundamental for V<sub>dc</sub> = 100 V.
quiz.a: sin 5d = 0 with d < 90° gives d = 72°, a 144° pulse. b<sub>1</sub> = (400/π) sin 72° = 127.3 × 0.9511 = 121.1 V peak.

quiz.q: Two square-wave bridges are phase-shifted by 60° and added through transformers. Which harmonic is removed, and why?
quiz.a: b<sub>n</sub> ∝ cos(nφ/2) = cos 30n°; for n = 3, cos 90° = 0, so the 3rd (and 9th) is removed. The sum is a 120° quasi-square wave.

quiz.q: Why is SHE attractive for megawatt drives and less so for small inverters?
quiz.a: Large devices must switch slowly; SHE removes the worst low harmonics with only a few switchings per cycle, so switching loss stays low. A small inverter can switch at tens of kilohertz, where sine PWM with a small filter is simpler than angle tables.

quiz.q: In the two-notch example, the 3rd and 5th are gone but the THD is not small. Explain.
quiz.a: The removed volt-seconds reappear at the 7th, 9th and 11th, which are now larger than in a plain square wave. SHE cleans the orders a filter finds hardest, not the whole spectrum.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern SHE solvers use homotopy and optimisation to find all solution sets, and selective harmonic mitigation limits harmonics to grid-code values instead of zero. Search for SHE-PWM, selective harmonic mitigation and twelve-pulse inverters.
